theory.question: Separate functional from nonfunctional requirements for a photo-sharing app, and explain why the nonfunctional ones still decide if the product is usable.
theory.answer:
Functional requirements are what the app does (upload a photo, follow a user, render a feed); nonfunctional requirements are properties of how it does it — fast, reliable, secure, legally compliant, maintainable.

For the photo app, functional requirements are the screens and operations: post a photo, like, comment, search. Nonfunctional requirements are usually unwritten because they seem obvious, but they are just as important: the feed must load quickly under expected load, uploads must not be lost, only authorized users may see private albums, and the system must stay maintainable as the team and features grow.

Four central nonfunctional concerns are performance, reliability, scalability, and maintainability. They matter because a perfectly featured app that loses a parent's only copies of their children's photos, or that takes ten seconds to open, fails its users regardless of feature completeness. Security adds further requirements, while performance, reliability, scalability, and maintainability remain central across data-system design.

Comment: These are the criteria you reason about when choosing tools and architectures; functional requirements tell you what to build, nonfunctional ones constrain how you build it and which trade-offs are acceptable.

theory.question: A social network gets 500M posts/day (5,800/s, spiking to 150k/s); the average user follows 200 and has 200 followers. Compare reading timelines on demand with a join versus precomputing them on write.
theory.answer:
Reading on demand re-runs an expensive multi-way join on every read; precomputing (materializing) each user's timeline on write turns reads into a cheap cache lookup at the cost of much more write work.

Two extreme cases break the simple version: a user following huge numbers of high-volume accounts gets a high write rate (acceptable to drop/sample, since they can't read it all), and a celebrity posting to millions of followers cannot have writes dropped — store celebrity posts separately and merge them at read time.

Comment: This hybrid (fan-out-on-write for most users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities) is the production-grade answer and the running example for the chapter's performance and scalability discussion.

theory.question: Define response time and throughput, and explain why response time spikes as throughput nears capacity.
theory.answer:
Response time is the elapsed time a user waits from request to answer; throughput is how many requests (or how much data) per second the system processes. As throughput approaches the hardware's capacity, response time rises sharply because of queueing.

A dangerous failure mode is metastable failure: under near-overload, slow responses cause clients to time out and retry, which raises load further — a retry storm — and the system can stay stuck overloaded even after the original load drops, until it is rebooted. Defenses include exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers or token buckets to stop hammering a failing service, load shedding (the server proactively rejecting requests when near overload), and backpressure (asking clients to slow down).

Comment: Response time is what users care about; throughput determines how much hardware (and cost) you need. A system is scalable if its max throughput can be significantly increased by adding resources.

theory.question: Distinguish latency, response time, service time, and queueing delay, and say why response time should be measured on the client side.
theory.answer:
Response time is the whole client-observed duration; service time is the part where the service is actively working; queueing delay is time spent waiting (e.g., for a CPU); latency is the catchall for any time the request is not being actively processed.

Response time varies request to request even for identical requests, due to context switches, lost packets and TCP retransmission, GC pauses, page faults forcing disk reads, even rack vibration. Queueing delay dominates much of this variability: because a server handles only a few requests in parallel, a few slow requests block later ones — head-of-line blocking — so even fast requests see a slow overall response time.

That head-of-line effect is exactly why you must measure on the client side: the queueing delay is not part of the server's service time, so server-side timers miss the time the client actually spent waiting.

theory.question: Why report response times as p50/p95/p99 percentiles instead of the average, and what is the tail-latency argument for caring about p99.9?
theory.answer:
Response time is a distribution with outliers, so the mean hides how many users actually suffer; percentiles tell you what fraction of requests beat a threshold, and high percentiles (tail latencies) directly shape the experience of your most valuable users.

Amazon specifies internal services at the 99.9th percentile even though it affects only 1 in 1,000 requests, because the slowest requests often belong to customers with the most data — the most valuable customers. Amazon also found optimizing the 99.99th percentile too expensive for too little benefit, since the extreme tail is dominated by random events outside your control.

Comment: Two practical warnings — averaging percentiles across machines or time windows is mathematically meaningless (aggregate by adding histograms, e.g., HdrHistogram or t-digest), and percentiles are the basis of SLOs/SLAs.

theory.question: A page fans out to profile, recommendations, permissions, and search services in parallel. Explain why its p99 can be worse than any single service's p99.
theory.answer:
Because the request must wait for the slowest of its parallel backend calls, even rare slow calls add up across many dependencies — an effect called tail latency amplification.

Even if each backend is individually fast, calling several of them in parallel means the user-facing response time is bounded by the worst one. If each service is slow on, say, 1% of calls, the probability that at least one of four parallel calls is slow is much higher than 1%, so a larger fraction of end-user requests end up slow than any single service's tail suggests. High percentiles therefore matter most precisely in fan-out backends.

This is why percentiles feed SLOs and SLAs: an SLO might target a median under 200 ms and a p99 under 1 second, plus 99.9% non-error responses; an SLA is the contract specifying consequences (like refunds) when the SLO is missed. Defining good availability metrics for these is itself nontrivial.

theory.question: Define a fault versus a failure, using a multi-disk storage node to show how the system boundary changes the label. Use a multi-disk storage node as the example.
theory.answer:
A fault is a component behaving incorrectly; a failure is the surrounding system no longer meeting its promised service. The distinction depends on the boundary under discussion.

Suppose a storage node contains four disks with redundancy. One disk dying is a fault inside the node. If reconstruction succeeds and reads and writes continue within the service objective, the node has not failed. If another disk dies before repair, corrupting data or making the node unavailable, the storage node has failed from the cluster's point of view. At the cluster boundary, that failed node may still be only a fault if replicas elsewhere keep the database available.

Reliable design expects component faults and contains them before they cross the system boundary. Monitoring detects the disk error, redundancy preserves service, repair restores safety margin, and the service-level objective defines when the overall outcome counts as a failure.

theory.question: Why would a reliable system deliberately kill its own processes (fault injection / chaos engineering)?
theory.answer:
Because fault-tolerance code only works if it actually runs, and deliberately injecting faults continuously exercises and tests the recovery path so it works when real faults occur.

The insight is counterintuitive: in a fault-tolerant system it can make sense to increase the rate of faults, for example by randomly killing processes without warning. Many critical bugs come from poor error handling, and an untested recovery path is likely to be broken precisely when you finally need it. Chaos engineering is the discipline built around this — running experiments such as deliberately injecting faults to build confidence in fault-tolerance mechanisms.

There is a limit to the prefer-tolerate-over-prevent stance: sometimes prevention is better because no cure exists. Security is the example — once an attacker has exfiltrated sensitive data, you cannot undo it — so prevention, not tolerance, is the goal there.

Comment: Netflix's Chaos Monkey popularized this; the modern practice is to run controlled fault-injection experiments in production with blast-radius limits and automated rollback.

theory.question: Compare hardware faults and software faults: which are correlated, and how does that change your defenses? Give concrete failure-rate numbers.
theory.answer:
Hardware faults are mostly independent and handled with redundancy; software faults are highly correlated across nodes (same code, same bug) and cause more system-wide failures, so redundancy alone does not help.

Hardware fault rates from the chapter: roughly 2%–5% of magnetic disks fail per year (≈one disk/day in a 10,000-disk cluster), 0.5%–1% of SSDs per year with uncorrectable errors about once/year/drive, about 1 in 1,000 machines has a CPU core that sometimes computes wrong results, and >1% of machines hit an uncorrectable RAM error per year even with ECC. These are largely independent, so RAID, dual power supplies, and especially distributing across machines/racks/availability zones tolerate them; cloud systems lean on software-level fault tolerance and rolling upgrades (patch one node at a time, no downtime).

Software faults are nastier because they are systematic: a leap-second kernel bug hung many Java services simultaneously; an SSD firmware bug bricked drives after exactly 32,768 hours; runaway processes exhaust shared resources; a slow dependency can trigger cascading failures. They lie dormant until an assumption about the environment stops holding. No quick fix — only testing, process isolation, crash-and-restart, avoiding retry storms, and monitoring in production.

theory.question: Operators making config changes are the leading cause of outages. How should a reliable system reduce human-error impact without treating the operator as the root cause?
theory.answer:
Treat operator mistakes as evidence that the system made a dangerous action too easy, not as the end of the investigation. Reliability improves when routine changes are automated, reviewed, observable, reversible, and limited in blast radius.

Useful safeguards include typed configuration with validation, dry runs, staged rollouts, canaries, automatic rollback on health regressions, separation of duties for high-risk actions, and an audit trail that shows who changed what. Destructive operations should require an explicit target and provide a recovery path. Runbooks and realistic staging environments help, but they cannot replace guardrails in production.

After an incident, a blameless review should examine interface design, missing checks, unclear ownership, alert quality, and recovery speed. The goal is to change the system so the same ordinary human slip no longer becomes an outage.

theory.question: Your startup founder argues that the company is not Google and should stop worrying about scale. When is that right, and when does scalability actually become your problem?
theory.answer:
Early on the founder is usually right — simplicity and flexibility beat hypothetical scale — but scalability becomes real once a measured load dimension is growing toward your architecture's limits.

Scalability is a system's ability to cope with increased load. For a young product with few users, premature scaling investment is wasted effort at best and an inflexible, hard-to-evolve design at worst; the goal is to keep things simple and adapt as you learn customers' needs. So the maxim holds — until your product succeeds and you start seeing where bottlenecks actually are.

Discussing scalability concretely means answering: if the system grows in a particular way, what are our options for coping; how do we add computing resources for the extra load; and based on current growth, when do we hit the limits of today's architecture. You first describe current load with the right load parameters — throughput (requests/s, GB/day, checkouts/hour), peak concurrent users, read/write ratio, cache hit rate, items per user (followers) — and note whether the average or the extreme cases dominate. Then ask what happens when a parameter doubles, both holding resources fixed and holding performance fixed. Doubling resources to handle double the load is linear scalability; more often cost grows faster than linearly.

theory.question: Contrast shared-memory (scale-up), shared-disk, and shared-nothing (scale-out) architectures, and the trade-offs of each.
theory.answer:
Shared-memory scales up one machine (simple but superlinear cost and a hard ceiling); shared-disk shares storage across machines over a fast network (limited by contention/locking); shared-nothing gives each node its own CPU, RAM, and disk (scales out linearly but adds distributed-systems complexity).

Cloud native databases blur this: separate storage and compute services let multiple compute nodes share a storage service, resembling shared-disk but using a specialized API rather than a filesystem/block-device abstraction, avoiding the old contention problems.

Comment: This is not a religious choice — good architectures use a pragmatic mixture, scaling a database up until cost, load, or availability force scale-out.

theory.question: Why is there no universal scaling recipe, and what general principles do help a fast-growing system scale?
theory.answer:
Because a scalable architecture is specific to the application's load parameters, no generic design exists; the durable principles are to break the system into independent components and to avoid unnecessary complexity.

The same throughput can demand utterly different designs: 100,000 requests/second of 1 kB each looks nothing like 3 requests/minute of 2 GB each, even though both move ~100 MB/s. And an architecture tuned for one load level usually cannot handle 10× that load, so a fast-growing service likely rethinks its architecture roughly every order of magnitude — meaning it's rarely worth planning more than one order of magnitude ahead.

Comment: This is why scalability work follows measured bottlenecks rather than speculation — you scale the dimension that is actually growing, when it is actually growing.

theory.question: Break maintainability into operability, simplicity, and evolvability, and explain accidental complexity, abstraction, and irreversibility.
theory.answer:
Maintainability has three practical dimensions: operability, simplicity, and evolvability.

Operability means the service is easy to monitor, diagnose, deploy, repair, and run within predictable limits. Good defaults, useful telemetry, automation, and clear failure modes reduce the amount of specialist knowledge required during an incident.

Simplicity means engineers can form an accurate model of the system. Remove accidental complexity such as duplicated state, inconsistent abstractions, and unnecessary custom infrastructure. A good abstraction hides implementation detail while preserving the distinctions callers need for correctness.

Evolvability means requirements and implementations can change without a risky rewrite. Stable interfaces, compatible schemas, tests, and reversible migrations keep future options open. Irreversible decisions deserve extra scrutiny because they constrain all later work. These properties reinforce one another: a comprehensible system is easier to operate and safer to change.

practice.task: [Python] Materialize home timelines with hybrid fan-out, quantifying write-time cost vs on-demand reads and handling celebrities.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ (stdlib only; no extra packages).

A social network gets about 500 million posts per day (≈5,800 posts/second). The average user follows 200 accounts and has 200 followers, but a few celebrities have millions of followers. About 10 million users are online and poll their home timeline every five seconds. Approach 1 rebuilds each timeline on every read by joining follows → posts. Approach 2 materializes timelines on write (fan-out into each follower's mailbox). Production systems use a hybrid: fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors, and fan-out-on-read (merge at read time) for celebrities.

This lab is an in-memory simulation. You will quantify the workload's cost argument with the load parameters above, then implement hybrid materialization (including the two extreme cases) in `timeline_lab.py`.

Save the file below as `timeline_lab.py`.

```python

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Set

# Chapter load parameters (use these in cost formulas)
POSTS_PER_SEC = 5_800
AVG_FOLLOWERS = 200
ONLINE_USERS = 10_000_000
POLL_INTERVAL_SEC = 5

# Lab thresholds for extreme cases
CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN = 10_000  # authors at/above this are celebrities
HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE = 500  # max non-celebrity followees to deliver into a power-user mailbox


@dataclass
class Post:
    post_id: int
    author_id: str
    ts: int
    text: str


@dataclass
class Network:
    followers: Dict[str, Set[str]] = field(default_factory=dict)  # author -> followers
    following: Dict[str, Set[str]] = field(default_factory=dict)  # user -> authors followed
    posts: List[Post] = field(default_factory=list)
    celebrity: Set[str] = field(default_factory=set)
    mailboxes: Dict[str, List[int]] = field(default_factory=dict)  # user -> post_ids newest-first
    celebrity_posts: Dict[str, List[int]] = field(default_factory=dict)  # author -> post_ids
    lookup_ops: int = 0
    write_ops: int = 0

    def add_follow(self, follower: str, author: str) -> None:
        self.followers.setdefault(author, set()).add(follower)
        self.following.setdefault(follower, set()).add(author)
        self.mailboxes.setdefault(follower, [])
        self.mailboxes.setdefault(author, [])

    def mark_celebrities(self) -> None:
        self.celebrity = {
            author
            for author, fans in self.followers.items()
            if len(fans) >= CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN
        }

    def read_on_demand(self, user_id: str, limit: int = 100) -> List[Post]:
        """Approach 1: join follows -> posts; counts each post row touch as a lookup."""
        authors = self.following.get(user_id, set())
        collected: List[Post] = []
        for author in authors:
            for p in self.posts:
                if p.author_id == author:
                    self.lookup_ops += 1
                    collected.append(p)
        collected.sort(key=lambda p: p.ts, reverse=True)
        return collected[:limit]

    def publish(self, author_id: str, ts: int, text: str) -> Post:
        post = Post(len(self.posts) + 1, author_id, ts, text)
        self.posts.append(post)
        self.fan_out_on_write(post)
        return post

    def fan_out_on_write(self, post: Post) -> None:
        # implement hybrid write path:
        # - if author is celebrity: append post_id to celebrity_posts[author] only (no mailbox fan-out)
        # - else: insert post_id at front of each follower mailbox and increment write_ops once per insert
        # - extreme (power user): if a follower follows more than HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE non-celebrity
        #   authors, only deliver posts from the first HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE of those authors
        #   (sorted by author_id); skip the rest (sample/drop)
        raise NotImplementedError

    def read_home(self, user_id: str, limit: int = 100) -> List[Post]:
        # implement hybrid read path:
        # - start from mailbox post_ids for user_id
        # - also merge celebrity_posts for every celebrity the user follows
        # - dedupe by post_id, sort by timestamp descending, return up to limit
        raise NotImplementedError


def approach1_lookups_per_sec() -> float:
    # implement: timeline queries/sec = ONLINE_USERS / POLL_INTERVAL_SEC;
    # return queries/sec * AVG_FOLLOWERS (post lookups/sec under Approach 1)
    raise NotImplementedError


def approach2_writes_per_sec() -> float:
    # implement: return POSTS_PER_SEC * AVG_FOLLOWERS (timeline mailbox writes/sec under Approach 2)
    raise NotImplementedError


def seed() -> Network:
    n = Network()
    normals = [f"u{i}" for i in range(20)]
    for u in normals:
        n.mailboxes.setdefault(u, [])

    celeb = "celeb"
    for u in normals:
        n.add_follow(u, celeb)
    for i in range(CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN):
        n.add_follow(f"fan{i}", celeb)

    for author in ("alice", "bob"):
        for u in normals:
            n.add_follow(u, author)

    power = "power"
    n.mailboxes.setdefault(power, [])
    for i in range(HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE + 50):
        n.add_follow(power, f"stream{i}")

    n.mark_celebrities()
    assert "celeb" in n.celebrity
    return n


def run_checks() -> None:
    a1 = approach1_lookups_per_sec()
    a2 = approach2_writes_per_sec()
    print(f"approach1_lookups_per_sec={a1:.0f}")
    print(f"approach2_writes_per_sec={a2:.0f}")
    print(f"write_path_cheaper_by_factor={a1 / a2:.1f}")

    n = seed()
    n.publish("alice", 1, "hi from alice")
    n.publish("bob", 2, "hi from bob")
    writes_before_celeb = n.write_ops
    n.publish("celeb", 3, "celebrity announce")
    assert n.write_ops == writes_before_celeb, "celebrity posts must not fan out to mailboxes"

        n.publish(f"stream{i}", 10 + i, f"stream {i}")
    assert len(n.mailboxes["power"]) <= HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE, "power-user mailbox must be sampled"

    home = n.read_home("u0")
    authors = {p.author_id for p in home}
    assert {"alice", "bob", "celeb"} <= authors, "hybrid read must merge mailbox + celebrity posts"
    print("checks_passed=true")
    print(f"power_mailbox_len={len(n.mailboxes['power'])}")
    print(f"u0_home_authors={sorted(authors)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_checks()
```

practice.answer:
Use the supplied workload parameters to show Approach 1 needs about 400 million post lookups/sec while Approach 2 needs about 1.16 million timeline writes/sec (≈345× cheaper work units). Implement hybrid materialization: fan-out-on-write for ordinary authors, store celebrity posts separately and merge them at read time, and sample deliveries for power users who follow too many non-celebrity streams.

Complete `timeline_lab.py`:

```python
# timeline_lab.py — full reference: hybrid materialized timelines
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Set

POSTS_PER_SEC = 5_800
AVG_FOLLOWERS = 200
ONLINE_USERS = 10_000_000
POLL_INTERVAL_SEC = 5

CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN = 10_000
HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE = 500


@dataclass
class Post:
    post_id: int
    author_id: str
    ts: int
    text: str


@dataclass
class Network:
    followers: Dict[str, Set[str]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    following: Dict[str, Set[str]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    posts: List[Post] = field(default_factory=list)
    celebrity: Set[str] = field(default_factory=set)
    mailboxes: Dict[str, List[int]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    celebrity_posts: Dict[str, List[int]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    lookup_ops: int = 0
    write_ops: int = 0

    def add_follow(self, follower: str, author: str) -> None:
        self.followers.setdefault(author, set()).add(follower)
        self.following.setdefault(follower, set()).add(author)
        self.mailboxes.setdefault(follower, [])
        self.mailboxes.setdefault(author, [])

    def mark_celebrities(self) -> None:
        self.celebrity = {
            author
            for author, fans in self.followers.items()
            if len(fans) >= CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN
        }

    def read_on_demand(self, user_id: str, limit: int = 100) -> List[Post]:
        authors = self.following.get(user_id, set())
        collected: List[Post] = []
        for author in authors:
            for p in self.posts:
                if p.author_id == author:
                    self.lookup_ops += 1
                    collected.append(p)
        collected.sort(key=lambda p: p.ts, reverse=True)
        return collected[:limit]

    def publish(self, author_id: str, ts: int, text: str) -> Post:
        post = Post(len(self.posts) + 1, author_id, ts, text)
        self.posts.append(post)
        self.fan_out_on_write(post)
        return post

    def fan_out_on_write(self, post: Post) -> None:
        if post.author_id in self.celebrity:
            self.celebrity_posts.setdefault(post.author_id, []).insert(0, post.post_id)
            return

        for follower in self.followers.get(post.author_id, set()):
            followees = self.following.get(follower, set())
            non_celeb = sorted(a for a in followees if a not in self.celebrity)
            if len(non_celeb) > HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE:
                allowed = set(non_celeb[:HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE])
                if post.author_id not in allowed:
                    continue
            self.mailboxes.setdefault(follower, []).insert(0, post.post_id)
            self.write_ops += 1

    def read_home(self, user_id: str, limit: int = 100) -> List[Post]:
        by_id = {p.post_id: p for p in self.posts}
        ids: List[int] = list(self.mailboxes.get(user_id, []))
        for author in self.following.get(user_id, set()):
            if author in self.celebrity:
                ids.extend(self.celebrity_posts.get(author, []))

        seen: Set[int] = set()
        merged: List[Post] = []
        for pid in sorted(ids, key=lambda i: by_id[i].ts, reverse=True):
            if pid in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(pid)
            merged.append(by_id[pid])
            if len(merged) >= limit:
                break
        return merged


def approach1_lookups_per_sec() -> float:
    timeline_queries = ONLINE_USERS / POLL_INTERVAL_SEC
    return timeline_queries * AVG_FOLLOWERS


def approach2_writes_per_sec() -> float:
    return POSTS_PER_SEC * AVG_FOLLOWERS


def seed() -> Network:
    n = Network()
    normals = [f"u{i}" for i in range(20)]
    for u in normals:
        n.mailboxes.setdefault(u, [])

    celeb = "celeb"
    for u in normals:
        n.add_follow(u, celeb)
    for i in range(CELEBRITY_FOLLOWER_MIN):
        n.add_follow(f"fan{i}", celeb)

    for author in ("alice", "bob"):
        for u in normals:
            n.add_follow(u, author)

    power = "power"
    n.mailboxes.setdefault(power, [])
    for i in range(HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE + 50):
        n.add_follow(power, f"stream{i}")

    n.mark_celebrities()
    assert "celeb" in n.celebrity
    return n


def run_checks() -> None:
    a1 = approach1_lookups_per_sec()
    a2 = approach2_writes_per_sec()
    print(f"approach1_lookups_per_sec={a1:.0f}")
    print(f"approach2_writes_per_sec={a2:.0f}")
    print(f"write_path_cheaper_by_factor={a1 / a2:.1f}")

    n = seed()
    n.publish("alice", 1, "hi from alice")
    n.publish("bob", 2, "hi from bob")
    writes_before_celeb = n.write_ops
    n.publish("celeb", 3, "celebrity announce")
    assert n.write_ops == writes_before_celeb, "celebrity posts must not fan out to mailboxes"

    for i in range(HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE + 50):
        n.publish(f"stream{i}", 10 + i, f"stream {i}")
    assert len(n.mailboxes["power"]) <= HEAVY_FOLLOW_SAMPLE, "power-user mailbox must be sampled"

    home = n.read_home("u0")
    authors = {p.author_id for p in home}
    assert {"alice", "bob", "celeb"} <= authors, "hybrid read must merge mailbox + celebrity posts"
    print("checks_passed=true")
    print(f"power_mailbox_len={len(n.mailboxes['power'])}")
    print(f"u0_home_authors={sorted(authors)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_checks()
```

Run:

```bash
python3 timeline_lab.py
```

Expected output includes:

```text
approach1_lookups_per_sec=400000000
approach2_writes_per_sec=1160000
write_path_cheaper_by_factor=344.8
checks_passed=true
power_mailbox_len=500
```

Ops notes: at these loads, materializing on write turns ~400M read lookups/s into ~1.16M write inserts/s, so the write-time path pays off when read volume dominates. Celebrities cannot use eager fan-out (100M+ mailbox inserts per post); mark them, store posts separately, and merge at read time. Power users who follow tens of thousands of high-volume accounts cannot consume every delivery, so sampling mailbox writes is acceptable.
